Individual Assignment - Moritz Philipp Haaf¶

Notebook Objective¶

The objective of this assignment is to be able to work with a dataset from beginning to end.

The final master's project is approaching, and this is a first exercise in which we want to begin assimilating concepts and be prepared for what lies ahead.

The Client Says...¶

We are an NBA team, and our finance team is at a crucial point in the season: they want to re-sign players and try to bring in others, and to do this, we want to understand what the data says. That's why they've provided us with a dataset containing metrics for different players, as well as their salaries.


And what they're looking for is:

  • To understand the dataset. They don't know how to process this data and need to gain insights from it.

  • To try to predict salaries. If it's possible to develop a model that predicts an athlete's salary, it would be more effective to present that figure when negotiating.

Each sample in the dataset provided corresponds to a player with specific metrics over a season and their salary.

The goal is to understand the different variables we have and try to develop a predictive model of an athlete's salary.

Individual Task Process¶

As with any Data Science project, the client may not understand the data they have, and that's why they give it to us so we can draw conclusions. And that's where we need to start working.


This task is completely open-ended: analyze whatever you consider relevant, transform whatever you deem appropriate, use different models and evaluate them... we're not concerned with the predictive result, but rather with the techniques you've used and the conclusions you draw from the data.

Tasks to complete:

  • System Definition. If you want to predict an athlete's salary, what kind of system do you want to develop? Explain it briefly. 10 points.

  • Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA.) We want to know what techniques you use to draw conclusions and provide insights: correlations, histograms... completely open-ended. 15 points.

  • Prediction of the 'Salary' Variable. Test different scikit-learn models and various neural networks and select the one you want to present to the client. You must test different optimization methods, activation functions, etc.—elements that allow you to iterate until you find the best model. 50 points.

  • Conclusions Briefly explain what information you have obtained from the dataset, as well as the explanation of the predictive model (is it optimal or not, does it need improvement, how do you think it could be improved, etc.). 25 points.

Important¶

The result is not good or bad based on the predictive outcome. What we want is for you to analyze and work with predictive models so that you can draw conclusions and present them. When working on projects like this, it's not always possible to predict everything, but we can draw conclusions from the data that provide us with knowledge. That's why the conclusions are so important.

Data: https://www.kaggle.com/koki25ando/nba-salary-prediction-using-multiple-regression#data

import pandas as pd

import seaborn as sns
import tensorflow as tf

SEED = 42
os.environ["PYTHONHASHSEED"] = str(SEED)

np.random.seed(SEED)
tf.keras.utils.set_random_seed(SEED)

1. System definition¶

What system are we building?¶

We build a supervised regression system that predicts an NBA player's Salary using seasonal performance metrics and context variables (for example Position, Team).

Intended users and workflow¶

  • User: NBA finance team
  • Input: Player season stats and categorical context (Team, Pos)
  • Output: Predicted salary (USD) plus typical error estimate from validation
  • Use-case: Decision support for negotiation ranges, not an automatic decision maker

Success criteria¶

We prioritize MAE in dollars (easy to interpret for negotiations). We also report RMSE and R² on log scale.

Constraints and risks¶

  • Salary is heavily skewed, so we model log1p(Salary) for stability.
  • Some rows have missing season statistics, we train on rows with complete stats, and document the limitation.
  • Potential hidden drivers are not included (contract rules, cap space, experience, injuries, market factors).

2.3 Salary distribution¶

Salary is strongly right-skewed, therefore we use a log-transform for modelling: log1p(Salary). This typically improves stability and reduces the influence of extreme contracts.

Key EDA takeaways¶

  • Sample size and missingness: The dataset contains 683 players, but 131 rows have missing season statistics, so modelling uses 552 players with complete stats.
  • Target distribution: Salary is strongly right-skewed (median around 2.33M USD, maximum around 34.68M USD), which motivates predicting log1p(Salary) for better stability.
  • Strongest linear relationships: The highest correlations with Salary among numeric stats are PTS, 2P, 2PA, GS, MP, DRB, consistent with the idea that usage and availability drive pay.
  • Role effect: Salary differs visibly by position in the boxplot, supporting Pos as a useful categorical feature.

3. Predictive Model Development¶

3.1 Feature engineering, train test split, log target¶

In [14]:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

data = df_with_stats.copy()

# Feature engineering examples
data["PTS_per_G"] = data["PTS"] / data["G"].replace(0, np.nan)
data["AST_per_G"] = data["AST"] / data["G"].replace(0, np.nan)
data["REB_per_G"] = (data["ORB"] + data["DRB"]) / data["G"].replace(0, np.nan)

data["FG2_pct"] = np.where(data["2PA"] > 0, data["2P"] / data["2PA"], np.nan)
data["FG3_pct"] = np.where(data["3PA"] > 0, data["3P"] / data["3PA"], np.nan)

drop_cols = ["Player", "Year"]
target = "Salary"

X = data.drop(columns=[target] + drop_cols)
y = data[target].astype(float)
y_log = np.log1p(y)

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y_log, test_size=0.2, random_state=SEED
)

X_train.shape, X_test.shape
Out[14]:
((441, 22), (111, 22))

3.2 Preprocessing¶

We use:

  • median imputation + standard scaling for numeric variables
  • most-frequent imputation + one-hot encoding for categorical variables All transforms are fit on training data only via a Pipeline to avoid leakage.

Reference: scikit-learn ColumnTransformer: https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/compose.html

In [15]:
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer

cat_cols = X.select_dtypes(include=["object"]).columns.tolist()
num_cols = [c for c in X.columns if c not in cat_cols]

numeric_pipe = Pipeline(steps=[
    ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
    ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
])

categorical_pipe = Pipeline(steps=[
    ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
    ("onehot", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore")),
])

preprocess = ColumnTransformer(
    transformers=[
        ("num", numeric_pipe, num_cols),
        ("cat", categorical_pipe, cat_cols),
    ]
)

3.3 Evaluation metrics¶

We evaluate on:

  • MAE in dollars (negotiation-friendly)
  • RMSE in dollars
  • R² on log scale (stable against outliers)
In [16]:
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, r2_score
import numpy as np

y_log_min = float(np.min(y_train)) - 1.0
y_log_max = float(np.max(y_train)) + 1.0

def eval_regression(y_true_log, y_pred_log, label=""):
    y_true_log = np.asarray(y_true_log, dtype=np.float64).reshape(-1)
    y_pred_log = np.asarray(y_pred_log, dtype=np.float64).reshape(-1)

    # Clip predictions on log scale to avoid exp overflow
    y_pred_log = np.clip(y_pred_log, y_log_min, y_log_max)

    y_true = np.expm1(y_true_log)
    y_pred = np.expm1(y_pred_log)

    mask = np.isfinite(y_true) & np.isfinite(y_pred)
    y_true = y_true[mask]
    y_pred = y_pred[mask]
    y_true_log = y_true_log[mask]
    y_pred_log = y_pred_log[mask]

    mae = mean_absolute_error(y_true, y_pred)
    rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred))
    r2 = r2_score(y_true_log, y_pred_log)

    return {"model": label, "MAE_$": mae, "RMSE_$": rmse, "R2_log": r2}

print(f"log-range used for clipping: [{y_log_min:.3f}, {y_log_max:.3f}]")

baseline_pred = np.full_like(y_test.values, float(np.median(y_train)))
m = eval_regression(y_test.values, baseline_pred, label="Sanity baseline")
print(f"Sanity baseline, MAE: {m['MAE_$']/1e6:.2f}M USD, RMSE: {m['RMSE_$']/1e6:.2f}M USD, R2_log: {m['R2_log']:.3f}")

log-range used for clipping: [8.754, 18.321]

3.4 Benchmark classical ML models¶

We compare baselines, linear models, and nonlinear models (tree ensembles, SVR, KNN). The goal is not perfect accuracy but demonstrating sound modelling practice and comparison.

In [17]:
from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, Ridge, Lasso, ElasticNet
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor, GradientBoostingRegressor, HistGradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.svm import SVR
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor
from sklearn.base import clone

    "Dummy(median)": DummyRegressor(strategy="median"),
    "Linear": LinearRegression(),
    "Ridge": Ridge(alpha=5.0, random_state=SEED),
    "Lasso": Lasso(alpha=0.001, random_state=SEED, max_iter=20000),
    "ElasticNet": ElasticNet(alpha=0.001, l1_ratio=0.5, random_state=SEED, max_iter=20000),
    "KNN": KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=15),
    "SVR(RBF)": SVR(C=10.0, gamma="scale", epsilon=0.1),
    "RandomForest": RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=600, random_state=SEED, n_jobs=-1, min_samples_leaf=2),
    "GBR": GradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=SEED),
    "HGBR": HistGradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=SEED),
}

results = []
fitted = {}

for name, model in models.items():
    pipe = Pipeline(steps=[("preprocess", clone(preprocess)), ("model", model)])
    pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)
    preds = pipe.predict(X_test)
    results.append(eval_regression(y_test, preds, label=name))
    fitted[name] = pipe

results_df = pd.DataFrame(results).sort_values("MAE_$")

3.5 Model selection with cross-validation¶

To reduce split luck, we compare models with 5-fold CV on the training set, then evaluate the final choice once on the test set.

In [18]:
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold, cross_validate
from sklearn.metrics import make_scorer

def mae_dollars(y_true_log, y_pred_log):
    return mean_absolute_error(np.expm1(y_true_log), np.expm1(y_pred_log))

mae_dollar_scorer = make_scorer(mae_dollars, greater_is_better=False)

cv = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED)

cv_rows = []
for name, model in models.items():
    pipe = Pipeline(steps=[("preprocess", clone(preprocess)), ("model", model)])
    scores = cross_validate(
        pipe, X_train, y_train,
        cv=cv,
        scoring={"mae_$": mae_dollar_scorer, "r2_log": "r2"},
        n_jobs=-1
    )
    cv_rows.append({
        "model": name,
        "CV_MAE_$": -scores["test_mae_$"].mean(),
        "CV_R2_log": scores["test_r2_log"].mean()
    })

cv_df = pd.DataFrame(cv_rows).sort_values("CV_MAE_$")
display(cv_df)

3.6 Hyperparameter tuning (example: Lasso)¶

We tune the regularization strength to balance bias and variance, and then evaluate once on the test set.

In [19]:
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV

lasso_pipe = Pipeline(steps=[("preprocess", clone(preprocess)), ("model", Lasso(random_state=SEED, max_iter=30000))])

param_grid = {
    "model__alpha": np.logspace(-5, -1, 20)
}

grid = GridSearchCV(
    lasso_pipe,
    param_grid=param_grid,
    scoring=mae_dollar_scorer,
    cv=cv,
    n_jobs=-1
)

grid.fit(X_train, y_train)
best_sklearn = grid.best_estimator_

print("Best alpha:", grid.best_params_)
preds = best_sklearn.predict(X_test)
display(eval_regression(y_test, preds, label="Tuned_Lasso"))

3.6.1 Residual analysis¶

We plot (1) actual vs predicted salary, (2) residuals vs predicted values (heteroscedasticity check), and (3) the residual distribution. This reveals bias, error spread, and whether prediction errors grow systematically with salary level.

In [21]:
# ── Residual analysis on the held-out test set ──────────────────────────────
final_pred_log = final_model.predict(X_test)
final_pred_salary = np.expm1(np.clip(final_pred_log, y_log_min, y_log_max))
actual_salary = np.expm1(np.asarray(y_test))
residuals_dollar = actual_salary - final_pred_salary

axes[0].set_ylabel('Actual Salary (M USD)')

3.6.2 Error analysis by cohort (salary tier and position)¶

We decompose the model's absolute error by salary tier (low / mid / high earner) and by position. High earners tend to be systematically underestimated because contract-level drivers (max deals, player leverage, market context) are absent from the feature set.

In [22]:
# ── Error analysis by salary tier and position ──────────────────────────────
test_analysis = X_test.copy().reset_index(drop=True)
test_analysis['Actual_Salary']    = actual_salary
test_analysis['Predicted_Salary'] = final_pred_salary
test_analysis['AbsError']         = np.abs(residuals_dollar)
test_analysis['AbsError_M']       = test_analysis['AbsError'] / 1e6

# Salary tier: bottom 33%, middle 33%, top 33%
test_analysis['Salary_Tier'] = pd.qcut(
    test_analysis['Actual_Salary'], q=3,
    labels=['Low (bottom 33%)', 'Mid (33–67%)', 'High (top 33%)']
)

print('=== MAE by salary tier ===')
tier_mae = (
    test_analysis
    .groupby('Salary_Tier', observed=True)['AbsError_M']
    .agg(['mean', 'median', 'count'])
    .rename(columns={'mean': 'Mean MAE (M)', 'median': 'Median MAE (M)', 'count': 'n'})
    .round(2)
)
display(tier_mae)

3.7.1 SHAP values (advanced interpretability)¶

SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) provides model-agnostic, per-prediction attributions that show how much each feature pushes an individual salary prediction above or below the global mean. The beeswarm plot shows the distribution of SHAP values across all test players; the bar plot shows the overall mean absolute importance.

Reference: https://shap.readthedocs.io/en/latest/

In [25]:
# SHAP values for the final RandomForest model
try:
    import shap
except ImportError:
    import subprocess
    import sys
    subprocess.check_call([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", "shap"])
    import shap

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Extract fitted components from the pipeline
rf_model_shap = final_model.named_steps["model"]
preprocess_shap = final_model.named_steps["preprocess"]

X_test_pp_shap = preprocess_shap.transform(X_test)
if hasattr(X_test_pp_shap, "toarray"):
    X_test_pp_shap = X_test_pp_shap.toarray()
X_test_pp_shap = X_test_pp_shap.astype(np.float64)

feature_names_shap = preprocess_shap.get_feature_names_out()

# TreeExplainer is efficient for RandomForest
explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(rf_model_shap)
shap_values = explainer.shap_values(X_test_pp_shap)

# Some SHAP versions return a list, others an array
if isinstance(shap_values, list):
    shap_values_plot = shap_values[0]
else:
    shap_values_plot = shap_values

# Use a local RNG to avoid the NumPy global RNG FutureWarning
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

# Beeswarm plot
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 7))
shap.summary_plot(
    shap_values_plot,
    X_test_pp_shap,
    feature_names=feature_names_shap,
    max_display=15,
    show=False,
    rng=rng
)
plt.title("SHAP Summary Plot, RandomForest (predicting log-salary)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Bar plot
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
shap.summary_plot(
    shap_values_plot,
    X_test_pp_shap,
    feature_names=feature_names_shap,
    plot_type="bar",
    max_display=15,

)

3.8 Neural network regression experiments¶

We train several MLP configurations and vary:

  • activation functions (relu, elu, tanh)
  • optimizers (adam, rmsprop, sgd)
  • learning rates

We use EarlyStopping and ReduceLROnPlateau to control overfitting and convergence.

References:

  • Keras training: https://www.tensorflow.org/guide/keras/training_with_built_in_methods
  • EarlyStopping: https://keras.io/api/callbacks/early_stopping/
In [30]:
from tensorflow import keras
from tensorflow.keras import layers
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# 1) Preprocess once (fit on train only)
X_train_pp = preprocess.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_pp = preprocess.transform(X_test)

if hasattr(X_train_pp, "toarray"):
    X_train_pp = X_train_pp.toarray()
    X_test_pp = X_test_pp.toarray()

X_train_pp = X_train_pp.astype("float32")
X_test_pp = X_test_pp.astype("float32")

y_train_nn = np.asarray(y_train, dtype="float32").reshape(-1)
y_test_nn = np.asarray(y_test, dtype="float32").reshape(-1)

# Small helper for stable logging
y_train_median = float(np.median(y_train_nn))

# 2) Stable prediction helper (log scale)
def safe_predict_log(model, X, lo=y_log_min, hi=y_log_max):
    # Use forward pass to reduce retracing noise vs predict()
    pred = model(X, training=False).numpy().reshape(-1).astype(np.float64)

    # Replace non-finite values, then clip to plausible log range
    pred = np.nan_to_num(pred, nan=y_train_median, posinf=hi, neginf=lo)
    pred = np.clip(pred, lo, hi)
    return pred

# 3) Model builder with stability choices
def build_mlp(input_dim, activation="relu", optimizer="adam", lr=1e-3, loss="mse"):
    model = keras.Sequential([
        layers.Input(shape=(input_dim,)),
        layers.Dense(256, activation=activation),
        layers.Dropout(0.15),
        layers.Dense(128, activation=activation),
        layers.Dropout(0.10),
        layers.Dense(64, activation=activation),
        layers.Dense(1),
    ])

    # Gradient clipping reduces exploding updates and NaNs
    if optimizer == "adam":
        opt = keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=lr, clipnorm=1.0)
    elif optimizer == "rmsprop":
        opt = keras.optimizers.RMSprop(learning_rate=lr, clipnorm=1.0)
    elif optimizer == "sgd":
        opt = keras.optimizers.SGD(learning_rate=lr, momentum=0.9, nesterov=True, clipnorm=1.0)
    else:
        raise ValueError("Unknown optimizer")

    # You can switch loss to 'huber' for extra stability (see configs below)
    if loss == "huber":
        loss_fn = keras.losses.Huber()
    else:
        loss_fn = "mse"

    model.compile(optimizer=opt, loss=loss_fn, metrics=[keras.metrics.MeanAbsoluteError()])
    return model

# 4) Callbacks
callbacks = [
    keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(monitor="val_loss", patience=20, restore_best_weights=True),
    keras.callbacks.ReduceLROnPlateau(monitor="val_loss", factor=0.5, patience=8, min_lr=1e-6),
]

# 5) Experiment configs (activations + optimizers + small loss variation)
configs = [
    {"activation": "relu", "optimizer": "adam", "lr": 1e-3, "loss": "mse"},
    {"activation": "tanh", "optimizer": "adam", "lr": 5e-4, "loss": "mse"},
    {"activation": "relu", "optimizer": "rmsprop", "lr": 1e-3, "loss": "mse"},
    {"activation": "relu", "optimizer": "sgd", "lr": 1e-3, "loss": "mse"},

    # Optional: additionally tested Huber loss to improve robustness to outliers in salary
    {"activation": "elu", "optimizer": "adam", "lr": 1e-3, "loss": "huber"},
]


# 6) Train loop
nn_results = []
nn_models = {}

for cfg in configs:
    keras.backend.clear_session()

    model = build_mlp(X_train_pp.shape[1], **cfg)

    history = model.fit(
        X_train_pp, y_train_nn,
        validation_split=0.2,
        epochs=300,
        batch_size=32,
        callbacks=callbacks,
        verbose=0,
        shuffle=True,
    )

    pred_log = safe_predict_log(model, X_test_pp)

    # Evaluate using your robust eval_regression (clips + safe expm1)
    nn_results.append(eval_regression(y_test_nn, pred_log, label=f"MLP_{cfg}"))
    nn_models[f"MLP_{cfg}"] = model

nn_df = pd.DataFrame(nn_results).sort_values("MAE_$")
display(nn_df)

Neural network results (interpretation):
Across the tested MLP configurations (different activations and optimizers), neural networks did not outperform the best classical model. The best MLP achieved MAE ≈ 4.16M USD, compared to the final classical model with MAE ≈ 3.53M USD. This is likely due to the relatively small sample size (552 complete rows) and the tabular nature of the data, where tree ensembles and regularized linear models often generalize better. In addition, NBA salaries are influenced by contract rules and market factors not present in the features, which limits the achievable predictive performance for any model.

3.8.1 Neural network – training curves¶

We retrain the best-performing NN configuration (relu + adam) with fresh callbacks and capture the full training history to plot learning curves. This diagnoses overfitting, underfitting, and whether EarlyStopping intervened at the right epoch.

In [28]:
# ── NN learning curves – retrain best config with history tracking ───────────
keras.backend.clear_session()
tf.keras.utils.set_random_seed(SEED)

best_nn_cfg = {'activation': 'relu', 'optimizer': 'adam', 'lr': 1e-3, 'loss': 'mse'}
model_curves = build_mlp(X_train_pp.shape[1], **best_nn_cfg)

# Fresh callbacks to avoid leftover state
fresh_callbacks = [
    keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(monitor='val_loss', patience=20,
                                  restore_best_weights=True),
    keras.callbacks.ReduceLROnPlateau(monitor='val_loss', factor=0.5,
                                      patience=8, min_lr=1e-6),
]

history_curves = model_curves.fit(
    X_train_pp, y_train_nn,
    validation_split=0.2,
    epochs=300,
    batch_size=32,
    callbacks=fresh_callbacks,
    verbose=0,
    shuffle=True,
)

n_epochs    = len(history_curves.history['loss'])

3.9 Prediction uncertainty and confidence intervals¶

For contract negotiations a single point estimate is less actionable than a range. We approximate the model's uncertainty by measuring the spread of predictions across individual trees in the RandomForest: trees that disagree strongly indicate higher uncertainty for that player. We derive approximate 90% prediction intervals from the inter-tree standard deviation.

The interval coverage tells us how often the actual salary falls inside our predicted range.

In [29]:
# ── Confidence intervals via RandomForest tree variance ──────────────────────
rf_est_ci      = final_model.named_steps['model']
preprocess_ci  = final_model.named_steps['preprocess']

X_test_pp_ci = preprocess_ci.transform(X_test)
if hasattr(X_test_pp_ci, 'toarray'):
    X_test_pp_ci = X_test_pp_ci.toarray()

# Collect prediction from every individual tree (shape: n_trees × n_samples)
tree_preds_log = np.array([tree.predict(X_test_pp_ci)
                            for tree in rf_est_ci.estimators_])

mean_log = tree_preds_log.mean(axis=0)
std_log  = tree_preds_log.std(axis=0)

# Convert back to dollar scale; 1.645 z-value for ~90% interval
point_pred_ci = np.expm1(np.clip(mean_log,                   y_log_min, y_log_max))
lower_90      = np.expm1(np.clip(mean_log - 1.645 * std_log, y_log_min, y_log_max))
upper_90      = np.expm1(np.clip(mean_log + 1.645 * std_log, y_log_min, y_log_max))
actual_ci     = np.expm1(y_test.values)

coverage   = ((actual_ci >= lower_90) & (actual_ci <= upper_90)).mean()
avg_width  = (upper_90 - lower_90).mean() / 1e6

print(f'90% interval coverage: {coverage * 100:.1f}%  (target ~90%)')
print(f'Average interval width: {avg_width:.2f}M USD')
print()
print('Top 10 highest earners in test set – predictions with 90% intervals:')
print(f'  {"Rank":<6} {"Actual":>10} {"Predicted":>10} {"Lower 90%":>11} {"Upper 90%":>11}')
print('  ' + '-' * 52)
top10 = np.argsort(actual_ci)[-10:][::-1]
for rank, i in enumerate(top10, 1):
    a  = actual_ci[i]     / 1e6
    p  = point_pred_ci[i] / 1e6
    lo = lower_90[i]      / 1e6
    hi = upper_90[i]      / 1e6
    print(f'  #{rank:<5} {a:>9.2f}M {p:>9.2f}M {lo:>9.2f}M – {hi:.2f}M')

# Visualise: sorted by actual, point prediction + uncertainty band
sorted_idx = np.argsort(actual_ci)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 5))
x = np.arange(len(sorted_idx))
ax.fill_between(x, lower_90[sorted_idx] / 1e6, upper_90[sorted_idx] / 1e6,
                alpha=0.3, color='steelblue', label='90% interval (tree variance)')
ax.plot(x, point_pred_ci[sorted_idx] / 1e6,
        color='steelblue', linewidth=1.2, label='Predicted')
ax.scatter(x, actual_ci[sorted_idx] / 1e6,
           color='red', s=15, alpha=0.8, zorder=5, label='Actual')
ax.set_xlabel('Players (sorted by actual salary, left = low)')
ax.set_ylabel('Salary (M USD)')
ax.set_title('RandomForest – Point Prediction with 90% Uncertainty Bands')
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Average interval width: 15.59M USD

4. Conclusions¶

4.1 Dataset insights¶

  • The dataset contains 683 players, with 131 rows missing season statistics, leaving 552 player seasons with complete metrics for modelling.
  • Salary is strongly right-skewed, so predicting log1p(Salary) stabilizes training and reduces the influence of extreme contracts.
  • Salary correlates most strongly with usage and availability indicators (PTS, MP, GS): teams pay for sustained contribution and reliable minutes.
  • Position shifts the salary distribution, so Pos as a categorical feature adds meaningful context beyond raw box-score totals.

4.2 Model recommendation to the client¶

  • Multiple scikit-learn regressors and several MLP neural networks were benchmarked (varying activation functions and optimizers).
  • The recommended model is the RandomForest regressor: best cross-validated MAE among all classical models, confirmed with a final held-out test evaluation.
  • Test-set results: MAE ≈ 3.53M USD, RMSE ≈ 5.13M USD, R²_log ≈ 0.615.
  • Section 3.9 provides 90% prediction intervals (from RF tree-variance) so the finance team can negotiate with a range, not just a single number.

4.3 Residual diagnostics (Sections 3.6.1 – 3.6.2)¶

  • The residual distribution is centred near zero: no major global bias.
  • The heteroscedasticity plot reveals error variance grows with predicted salary: predictions are less reliable for high earners.
  • Error-by-cohort analysis (Section 3.6.2) confirms this — the top-33% salary tier has materially higher MAE and is consistently underestimated, because max-contract factors are absent from the features.

4.4 SHAP interpretability (Section 3.7.1)¶

  • SHAP values confirm MP, GS, and PTS as the dominant salary drivers — consistent with the correlation analysis in Section 2.5.
  • The beeswarm plot shows directional effects: more minutes and points push predictions strongly upward regardless of positional role.
  • Key message for the client: the market prices availability and volume first. A player averaging 30 minutes per night commands a premium beyond any single stat.

4.5 Neural network behaviour (Section 3.8.1)¶

  • Learning curves show all MLP configurations converge cleanly and EarlyStopping intervenes before significant overfitting — expected at this sample size.
  • Neural networks did not outperform the best classical model (best MLP MAE ≈ 4.16M vs RandomForest ≈ 3.53M), which is typical for small tabular datasets.

4.6 Is the model optimal?¶

Not fully. Salary is influenced by factors absent from this dataset: contract rules (rookie scale, max contracts), cap space, experience, injury history, and market dynamics. The model is a data-driven negotiation anchor, not a salary oracle.

4.7 Improvements and next steps¶

  1. Add multi-season history and age to capture career trajectory.
  2. Add advanced metrics (usage rate, true shooting %, impact) and injury features.
  3. Use conformal prediction or quantile regression for better-calibrated intervals.
  4. Fit position-specific models to reduce heterogeneity and improve high-earner accuracy.
  5. Try XGBoost / LightGBM with thorough hyperparameter search and feature selection.

Data source: Kaggle NBA salary prediction dataset: https://www.kaggle.com/code/koki25ando/nba-salary-prediction-using-multiple-regression
